extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, logicians, and scientists designing scientific language, nomenclature, or classifications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating precise, complete, and useful scientific terminology, nomenclature, and classifications so as to aid induction, memory, and discovery across the sciences. Covers criteria for words (terminology/nomenclature), the form of language relative to subject-matter, and principles of scientific (natural) classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology suited for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminology suited for describing with precision the individual facts observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology should enable definite, precise statements of observed particulars (examples: terms in botany like 'linear', 'lanceolate', 'serrated'). It is one of the principal requisites of a philosophical language (precision/definiteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names for every common property (terms for classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a name for every common property of any importance or interest which we detect by comparing facts; including names for the classes we artificially construct in virtue of those properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete general names where frequent predication occurs so that those properties become readily recallable and usable in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature: a name for every Kind (lowest Kind/infima species)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nomenclature must provide a name for every Kind — classes distinguished not by one or a few definite properties but by an indefinite multitude of them (lowest Kinds or infimæ species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every lowest Kind (e.g., species in natural history) should have a systematic name assigned, and new lowest Kinds should be named uniformly when discovered. Good examples: Linnaean biological nomenclature and modern chemical nomenclature; lack of systematic nomenclature (e.g., mineralogy) retards progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words in nomenclature must connote Kind and diagnostic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Words belonging to a nomenclature connote both (1) certain descriptive properties and (2) that those properties are distinctive of a Kind (i.e., that the name denotes a lowest Kind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The set of characters used to discriminate each Kind (the diagnostic characters) together with the form of the name constitute the meaning. Definitions (enumerated characters) plus the nomenclatural form convey the signification; if a supposed 'species' is found to be multiple Kinds, the name must be reapportioned to a true lowest Kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning must be preserved yet allow redefinition when taxonomy changes
rubrics_metrics.description: While the connoted diagnostic characters may be revised, the denotation as a Kind should be maintained insofar as possible; reforming the connotation need not change the intended denotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is often desirable to adjust the set of descriptive characters for practical distinction without altering the name's reference to the same lowest Kind, but one must recognise that meaning is conveyed by both definition and the nominal form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of language (names for all relevant Kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Completeness: in addition to precision, a philosophical language should be as complete as possible — e.g., have names for all Kinds with which a branch of knowledge is conversant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness may require constructing a systematic nomenclature (naming all lowest Kinds) so that newly discovered entities can be named on a uniform principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt language form to the mode of reasoning (mechanical when safe, obstructive when needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the nature of the subject permits reasoning to be carried on mechanically, the language should be constructed on as mechanical principles as possible; where mechanical use is dangerous, the language should be constructed to make merely mechanical use difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use highly symbolic, compact notation (like algebra) only for domains reducible to number-relations; for other sciences, ensure words retain meaning so that the mind cannot perform reasoning by rote without attending to the phenomena. The algebraic ideal is perfect for arithmetic/number relations but inappropriate when additional empirical specifics may alter applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximise semantic content of words to keep meaning in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: As much meaning as possible should be thrown into the formation of the word itself so that derivation and analogy keep alive a consciousness of what is signified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer word-formation from productive native roots and fixed analogies (examples: German and especially Greek roots) rather than arbitrary or borrowed forms; compound/derivative formation should reflect relations between ideas to prevent words becoming empty counters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid degeneration of terms into mere counters; maintain empirical engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms, however well constructed, tend to lose apparent meaning through use; to prevent this, practitioners must continually refresh meaning by habitual contemplation of the phenomena, not by living among formulae alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on formulas; keep up acquaintance with empirical realities to avoid misapplication of rules and to keep diagnostic sense of terms intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification as ordering to aid memory and discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification should be a contrivance for the best possible ordering of ideas so as to give the greatest command over acquired knowledge and to lead most directly to acquiring more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange groups and the order of groups to best conduce to remembrance and to ascertainment of laws; classification for this purpose considers real existing objects (not merely imaginable ones) and ideally embraces all really existing objects relevant to the domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose classificatory properties that indicate many and important commonalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer properties which are causes of many other properties or which are sure marks of them; classification should group objects according to attributes that lead to many and important general propositions about the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the causal property cannot be used diagnostically, select effects that reliably mark the cause; avoid artificial groupings based on trivial or arbitrary features that don't support broader generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural (scientific) classification over technical/artificial arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific or natural classification groups objects so that a greater number of important propositions can be made about the group than would be possible under other groupings; it often links to the general aspect and important properties of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural classifications may rely on unobvious but important properties; ensure there are recognisable marks (diagnostic characters) that coexist with these properties so observers can determine group membership without destroying the object (example: external integuments in Blainville's zoological classification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must consider the whole range of real objects
rubrics_metrics.description: No class can be properly constituted without taking into consideration all varieties of existing objects which have any affinity with it; classification of any group must be made in reference to a general division of the whole of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good systematics (e.g., families, genera) depend on embedding specific groupings into a comprehensive framework covering the relevant domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifications should be purposive (tailored to intended use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of a property for classification is relative to the end in view; different sciences or arts legitimately form different classifications of the same objects according to their special purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept multiple valid classifications for different practical ends (e.g., farmer: useful plants vs weeds; botanist: dicotyledon vs monocotyledon; geologist: fossils by strata). When studying for general knowledge, prefer classifications that capture the most significant and numerous shared properties (natural groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural groups (types) may be given by Type rather than strict Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural groups often are 'given by Type, not by Definition'—their characters are frequently stated as usual or general rather than universal, and descriptions may tolerate anomalies that contradict a strict definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and tolerate looseness or indecision in diagnostic characters for natural families; diagnostic (artificial) characters may be imperfect and sometimes yield to overall natural affinities when composing taxonomic judgments.
